issues.legal_issue: A court should not set aside a government lease without a cogent basis merely because the government is willing to annul it.
material_facts: A government lease was granted to a tenderer.
The reviewing court set aside the lease principally because the government said it was prepared to annul it if the court so directed.
The leaseholder did not concur in setting aside the lease.
The reviewing court gave no other cogent reason for cancelling the lease.
issues.conclusion: The reviewing court was not justified in setting aside the lease on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: A government’s willingness to set aside a lease does not, without the concurrence of the person primarily affected or another cogent reason, provide a valid basis for cancelling it.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_order and government_willing_to_cancel_lease and leaseholder_did_not_concur and no_other_cogent_basis

predicates.appeal_from_writ_order: The case is an appeal from an order made in a writ proceeding.
predicates.government_willing_to_cancel_lease: The government told the reviewing court that it was prepared to cancel the lease if the court directed it to do so.
predicates.leaseholder_did_not_concur: The person holding the lease did not agree to its cancellation.
predicates.no_other_cogent_basis: The reviewing court relied on no other cogent basis for cancelling the lease.
predicates.lease_cancellation_without_cogent_basis_: A lease should not be cancelled without a cogent basis.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a writ order concerns a lease the government was willing to cancel, the leaseholder did not agree, and no other cogent basis was given, the cancellation is unjustified.

issues.legal_issue: A government may reserve discretion to reject the highest tender or select another tender, and is not bound to accept the highest tender, provided its decision is not vitiated by mala fides or reviewable arbitrariness.
material_facts: The government invited sealed tenders for a lease and stated that the highest tender would ordinarily be accepted but that it could select any tender or reject all tenders without giving a reason.
One tender was higher than the leaseholder’s original tender.
The leaseholder was asked to raise its offer and did so, offering more than the highest original tender.
The lease was granted to the leaseholder, and the highest original tender was not accepted.
The challenging tenderer did not allege mala fides, and the grant was not shown to be vitiated by arbitrariness warranting judicial interference.
issues.conclusion: The reservation of discretion was not contrary to Article 14, and the government was not required to accept the highest tender; the grant was not shown to warrant judicial interference.
issues.legal_principle: In government contracting, a condition reserving the right to select any tender or reject all tenders is not, by itself, contrary to Article 14, and the government need not accept the highest tender. The Court relied on C.K. Achuthan v. State of Kerala, Trilochan Mishra v. State of Orissa, State of Orissa v. Harinarayan Jaiswal, Cooverjee B. Bharucha’s case, and Union of India v. M/s Bhimsen Walaiti Ram. It distinguished Century Spinning & Manufacturing Co. v. Ulhasnagar Municipal Council, Rashbihar Panda v. State of Orissa, Dwarka Prasad Laxmi Narain v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Guruswamy v. State of Mysore. The general principles in the relied-on cases applied even though those cases involved statutory provisions.

rule.if: government_contract_tender_case and tender_terms_reserve_selection_or_rejection and highest_original_tender_not_accepted and no_mala_fides_or_reviewable_arbitrariness

predicates.government_contract_tender_case: The proceeding concerns the government’s choice of a tender for a contract or lease.
predicates.tender_terms_reserve_selection_or_reject: The tender terms state that the government may select a tender or reject all tenders rather than invariably accept the highest tender.
predicates.highest_original_tender_not_accepted: The government does not accept the highest original tender.
predicates.no_mala_fides_or_reviewable_arbitrarines: No mala fides are alleged or the decision is not shown to involve arbitrariness warranting judicial interference.
predicates.government_need_not_accept_highest_tende: The government need not accept the highest tender, and reserving discretion to select or reject tenders is not, by itself, unconstitutional.

issues.definition: In a government tender case, where the terms reserve selection or rejection, the highest original tender is not accepted, and no mala fides or reviewable arbitrariness is shown, the government need not accept the highest tender and the reservation is not unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: A rule governing the auction of a government lease does not govern a lease process conducted by invitation of sealed tenders rather than by auction.
material_facts: The government invited sealed tenders for the lease of a distillery.
The lease process was conducted by invitation of tenders, not by public auction.
The relied-on provision concerned putting the lease to auction in stipulated circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The auction provision did not govern the lease process because the government invited tenders rather than holding an auction.
issues.legal_principle: An auction is a sale or letting by bids, usually to the highest bidder through public competition; an invitation to tender is an attempt to obtain offers and is an invitation to negotiate. The Court relied on Article 9, paragraph 2, of Legislative Diploma No. 1761 and the descriptions in Halsbury’s Laws of England, Third Edition, Volume 2, pages 69 and 422.

predicates.government_lease_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the government’s grant of a lease.
predicates.sealed_tenders_invited: The government invited prospective lessees to submit sealed offers.
predicates.no_public_auction: The lease was not offered through public bidding at an auction.
predicates.auction_only_lease_rule_does_not_govern_: A rule that applies to an auction does not govern a lease process conducted by invitation of tenders.

issues.definition: Where a government lease proceeding involves sealed tenders and no public auction, an auction-only rule does not govern the tender process.
